newsitem.title: USA: Fujimori birthplace issue fuels Peru woes--Wall St.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori birthplace issue fuels Peru woes--Wall St.

text.p: Opposition press reports that Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori may have been born in Japan sent a warning that the country's political crisis was deepening, U.S. investors said Friday.

"This should create some concern whether we're seeing a breakdown of the forces associated with the reform process, but that is not the reaction in the marketplace," said Ali Naqvi, portfolio manager at Citibank Global Asset Management.
Naqvi added that international investors seemed to be brushing off the warning signs of turmoil in Peru, viewing any dips in price as an opportunity to pick up yield.

Peruvian debt prices held firm this week amid an overall emerging market bond rally, but the country's paper slumped on Friday. Peru PDI bonds dropped 1-1/4 to 64-3/4 and FLIRBs lost 1-1/2 points to 58-3/4.
A government spokesman had no comment on the allegations of Fujimori's birthplace. Peru's constitution requires a president to be born in that country.

Fujimori's popularity has plummeted in recent weeks to its lowest point since he took office in 1990, and a series of scandals involving alleged abuses of power by the security forces have sparked violent street protests.

Public concern over allegations of torture and abuse by security agents turned to outrage last week when the government revoked the Peruvian citizenship of Israeli-born businessman Baruch Ivcher just before his television station aired a report on systematic phone-tapping by security agents.

"To me, it smells like Bucaram all over again," one U.S. portfolio manager said, in reference to the political crisis in neighboring Ecuador that forced its President Abdala Bucaram to resign earlier this year.

"Fujimori took the citizenship of this guy Ivcher, so he has in a way legitimized the question of nationality," the fund manager added. "It's an explosive issue in Peru and I think the Americans are missing it."

But other U.S. fund managers played down the significance of Peru's current turmoil, given that international investors seemed determined to achieve higher returns in a climate of global liquidity and low interest rates.
"Clearly, political risk is rising in Peru, but whether it will have a significant impact, I don't think so," said Frank Fernandez, principal portfolio manager at Global Emerging Markets Advisors.
Peruvian paper had gained Thursday as the entire Brady bond market rallied after Ecuador received a B1 sovereign rating from Moody's Investors Service Inc.
Moody's placed Ecuador at a higher level than Peru, and the agency said last week that politics presented the main constraint to Peru's B2 rating.
